doc.title: Doug Carn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 24, 2023

title: Soloists unpaid for their improvised compositions
summary: Carn argues improvisers are composers who get no writer's credit while publishers and labels collect, citing Morello, Gonsalves and Coltrane.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: But so I said, “Man, you know something? Y’all don’t know nothing about music” you know. They said, “Who do you think you are, a little Negro from St. Augustine, Florida you know. You don’t know diddly.” I said, “I might not but I know about music. You all don’t know nothing about music” you know then I bowed my head and backed off you know. But you know that’s the thing, you know so, but then yeah, I realized you improvised but actually Gary Bartz taught me this, you’re not really improvising, you’re a composer you know. It’s just quick work. Just like spontaneous artwork you know, when they’re painting a picture, just painting it fast, but it’s like [scats] you know? You’re not really — you know you’re creating, you’re actually writing music. And that’s another beef that I got with the industry. You know you do a song and the soloist don’t get paid for what they’re doing. They say, “Brubeck wrote it — Green wrote the tune, Coleman Hawkins just played it.” But see when you buy a jazz record you buy the record to hear what solos the guys took you know? Not just two chords inside the melody. You know what I’m saying?
Right. You’re not getting any writer’s credit for the improvising.
Right. So they’d do “Take Five” all right? And in that solo that Joe Morello took, he don’t get no money for that. You know what I’m saying?

Those 52 choruses of “Crescendo and Diminuendo” that Paul Gonzalves played, he don’t get no money for that, you know what I mean? And all the great solos with all that stuff, Trane played on “My Favorite Things,” You know Rodgers, Hammerstein get all of that money you know, as if they wrote it. You know? And but see where it came from was way back in the day before “Bye-Bye Blackbird” and them other songs, and “Tiger Rag” and stuff. You know you’d play the record and then the little stuff you did in between like an ad lib wasn’t that considerable even though it was they just let that go and passed that on, but you’re still playing Irving Berlin’s song you know. But after the swing era came
in, and especially bebop, they started adding more music to the composition than the composition had in the first place. You know what I’m saying?

And so but they don’t get paid for that. You know? See actually I’m not being bitter or have an attitude about it, but record companies owe the jazz musicians half of all the money they made, the publishing companies too you know. Because they copyrighted and collected money through performance rights organizations of music that they did not create you know. If they was only going to get paid for owning the melody then you don’t need other stars to play you know? Just get a drum machine to keep the beat and let Oscar Peterson play you know? And then but they’ve got to have George Duvivier or Ray Brown to fill in in the rhythm section making the sound groovy you know. And the publisher would get more money than Oscar Peterson, he’d get double or triple if you’re smart as Ray Charles you’d get ten times as much as a sideman or whatever. But there’s so many holes in it. This is why a lot of educated people wouldn’t be a musician, wouldn’t be in the music business. Because they have studied it thoroughly you know, and it’s always for somebody that’s got ego enough, you know, to want to be up there on the stage with people clapping for them and girls swooning you know. But to some of us there’s a duty too, you know, because we realize that the people need culture, and music and culture and dance is for the betterment of society and the well being of the people.
